_meta.comment: Original KaiSip CSOE practice questions for Domain 3 (Corporate responsibility and financial disclosure), written from the public law (the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the U.S. Code and SEC rules and releases) and KaiSip's own notes (data/csoe/notes/d3.json). No SOXCPA material was used. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the Sarbanes Oxley Compliance Professionals Association (SOXCPA). Schema: docs/content/QUESTION_SCHEMA.md; writing rules: docs/content/EXAM_STYLE_V2.md and .claude/agents/csoe-standards-auditor.md. Pilot csoe_d3_001 to csoe_d3_020, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Audit committees. Member eligibility
questions.question: A listed company's board wants a director on its audit committee who also earns a consulting fee from a company subsidiary. Under Rule 10A-3, which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The director may serve once shareholders are told about the fee
options.B: The director may serve only after the fee arrangement ends
options.C: The director may serve because they are not a company employee
options.D: The director may serve because a subsidiary, not the issuer, pays

questions.key_concept: An audit committee member may take no consulting, advisory or other compensatory fee from the issuer or any subsidiary.
questions.pre_read: Recall which payments Rule 10A-3 lets a committee member receive, and from which companies in the group.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10A-3 bars an audit committee member from accepting any consulting, advisory or other compensatory fee, directly or indirectly, from the issuer or any subsidiary, other than for board and committee service. The consulting fee therefore disqualifies the director while it continues. Option D fails because the rule names subsidiaries expressly, so which company in the group pays makes no difference.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disclosure fixes many governance gaps. But independence is a listing condition; telling shareholders about the fee does not make the director independent.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because employees plainly lack independence. But Rule 10A-3 also bars consulting and advisory fees and affiliate status, so non-employees can fail too.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the fee does come from a subsidiary. But Rule 10A-3 covers fees from the issuer or any subsidiary, so the payer changes nothing.

tips: Eliminate: A and C. Disclosure does not cure a failed independence test, and Rule 10A-3 looks beyond employment to any consulting or advisory fee.
Final two: B beats D because the fee ban covers payments from the issuer or any of its subsidiaries.
Exam cue: for audit committee independence, any non-board fee from the company group disqualifies the member, whatever the amount or which entity pays.
questions.framework_ref: 17 CFR 240.10A-3(b)(1) (Audit committee member independence); Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 301 (Public company audit committees)

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Audit committees. Accounting dispute
questions.question: At a listed company, the CFO and the external audit firm disagree on when to recognize revenue from a large contract. Under Section 301, who has PRIMARY responsibility for resolving the disagreement?

options.A: The CFO, who prepares the financial statements
options.B: The PCAOB, which inspects and disciplines the audit firm
options.C: The full board of directors, which appoints the committees
options.D: The audit committee, which oversees the audit firm's work

questions.key_concept: The audit committee oversees the auditor's work, including resolving financial reporting disagreements between management and the auditor.
questions.pre_read: Identify which body Section 301 makes directly responsible for the auditor's work, and what that oversight includes.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 301 makes the audit committee, acting as a committee of the board, directly responsible for overseeing the audit firm's work, including resolving disagreements between management and the auditor about financial reporting. The firm reports directly to the committee. A listed company must have an audit committee, and the Act places this duty on that committee rather than on the board as a whole.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the CFO prepares the numbers in dispute. But the CFO is one side of the disagreement; Section 301 gives its resolution to the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the PCAOB oversees audit firms. But it inspects and disciplines firms; it does not settle a company's accounting disputes with its auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the audit committee is a committee of the board. But Section 301 assigns oversight of the auditor, including disputes, directly to the audit committee.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. The CFO is one side of the dispute, and the PCAOB regulates audit firms rather than resolving a client's reporting disagreements.
Final two: D beats C because Section 301 places oversight of the auditor, including management-auditor disputes, on the audit committee itself.
Exam cue: hiring, paying, overseeing or refereeing the outside auditor points to the audit committee, not management or the whole board.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Audit committees. Employee concerns
questions.question: An employee at a listed company wants to report questionable accounting without giving their name. Which channel does Section 301 MOST directly require the audit committee to provide?

options.A: Confidential, anonymous submission of concerns by employees
options.B: A hotline the external auditor runs for employee concerns
options.C: An internal audit team that investigates each employee concern
options.D: A reporting line that sends employee concerns straight to the SEC

questions.key_concept: Audit committees must set procedures for accounting complaints and for employees' confidential, anonymous submission of concerns.
questions.pre_read: Recall which body owns the complaint procedures and what employees must be able to do through them.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 301 requires each audit committee to set procedures for the confidential, anonymous submission by employees of concerns about questionable accounting or auditing, alongside procedures for complaints the company receives. The committee owns the procedures; staff or a vendor may run them. SOX itself does not require an internal audit function, so an internal audit team is not what the section demands.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the auditor is independent of management. But Section 301 puts the procedures under the audit committee, not the external audit firm.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: internal audit often helps investigate. But Section 301 requires audit committee procedures for anonymous submission; SOX does not itself require an internal audit function.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC receives tips. But that is a separate whistleblower route; Section 301 requires an internal channel set by the audit committee.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Section 301 places the channel under the audit committee, so neither the outside auditor's hotline nor a line to the SEC is what it requires.
Final two: A beats C because the section requires confidential, anonymous submission procedures, and SOX does not mandate an internal audit function.
Exam cue: anonymous employee concerns about accounting point to the audit committee's Section 301 complaint procedures.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Disclosures behind the signature
questions.question: Before signing the quarterly Section 302 certification, a CFO learns that the assistant controller, who approves journal entries, took $8,000 from petty cash, an immaterial amount. What is the MOST accurate requirement?

options.A: Leave it out of the disclosures, since the amount is immaterial
options.B: Report it in the Section 906 statement furnished with the report
options.C: Disclose it to the auditors and the audit committee
options.D: Disclose it in the quarterly report as a material weakness

questions.key_concept: Officers disclose to the auditors and audit committee any fraud, material or not, involving management or key internal control staff.
questions.pre_read: Note the employee's role in internal control, then recall what the certification says officers have disclosed, and to whom.
questions.correct_explanation: The Section 302 certification states that the signing officers have disclosed to the auditors and the audit committee any fraud, whether or not material, involving management or other employees with a significant role in internal control. An assistant controller who approves journal entries has that role. The rule calls for disclosure to those two parties; it does not turn an immaterial theft into a publicly reported material weakness.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because most disclosure turns on materiality. But the 302 certification covers fraud by key control staff whether or not it is material.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because 906 is also an officer certification. But the 906 statement covers compliance and fair presentation, not reporting fraud to anyone.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the theft may signal a control deficiency. But the certification requires disclosure to the auditors and audit committee; it does not label this a material weakness.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. The 302 duty covers fraud by key control staff even when immaterial, and the 906 statement contains no fraud disclosure.
Final two: C beats D because the certification sends insider fraud to the auditors and audit committee without making an immaterial theft a public material weakness.
Exam cue: fraud by management or key control staff, material or not, goes to the auditors and audit committee under Section 302.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Penalty tier
questions.question: A CEO willfully certifies a Section 906 statement knowing the periodic report does not comply with the Exchange Act. What is the GREATEST criminal penalty the statute allows?

options.A: Up to $1 million in fines and 10 years in prison
options.B: Up to $5 million in fines and 20 years in prison
options.C: Repayment of bonuses received in the following 12 months
options.D: A civil money penalty and a bar from serving as an officer

questions.key_concept: Section 906 has two criminal tiers: knowing certification up to $1 million and 10 years; willful up to $5 million and 20 years.
questions.pre_read: Find the word in the stem that tells you which of the statute's two penalty tiers applies.
questions.correct_explanation: 18 U.S.C. 1350, added by Section 906, has two penalty tiers. Knowingly certifying a noncompliant report carries fines up to $1 million, prison up to 10 years, or both. Willfully certifying it, as here, carries fines up to $5 million, prison up to 20 years, or both. The word willfully in the stem selects the higher tier.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this is the 906 penalty for knowing certification. Willful certification moves to the higher tier of $5 million and 20 years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because repayment follows misconduct restatements. But that is Section 304, a civil reimbursement duty, not the criminal penalty for a false 906 certification.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC can seek bars and civil penalties. But the question asks for the criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. 1350, which means fines and prison.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Bonus repayment is Section 304 and bars are civil remedies, while Section 906 sets criminal fines and prison.
Final two: B beats A because willful certification carries the higher tier; $1 million and 10 years applies to knowing certification.
Exam cue: for Section 906, knowing means up to $1 million and 10 years; willful means up to $5 million and 20 years.
questions.framework_ref: 18 U.S.C. 1350(c) (Criminal penalties)

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Quarterly filing contents
questions.question: Preparing a Form 10-Q, a CFO plans to attach Section 302 and 906 certifications and include a Section 404 management report on internal control. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Drop the 404 report, which goes with the annual report alone
options.B: Drop the 906 statement, which goes with the annual report alone
options.C: Drop the 302 certification, which goes with the annual report alone
options.D: Keep the three items, since each is required in every quarterly report

questions.key_concept: Sections 302 and 906 certifications go with quarterly and annual reports; the Section 404(a) management report is annual only.
questions.pre_read: For each of the three items, recall which periodic reports the statute names.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(a) requires management's internal control report in each annual report only, so it does not belong in a Form 10-Q. Section 302 covers each annual and quarterly report, and Section 906 (18 U.S.C. 1350) covers every periodic report containing financial statements, which includes a 10-Q. Both certifications stay; only the 404 report comes out.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: some link the criminal 906 statement to the 10-K alone. But 18 U.S.C. 1350 covers every periodic report with financial statements, including a 10-Q.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because annual reports carry the most certifications. But Section 302 expressly covers each annual or quarterly report.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because all three are SOX duties. But Section 404(a) asks for management's internal control report in the annual report, not each quarter.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 302 names quarterly reports expressly, and the Section 404 management report is an annual requirement.
Final two: A beats B because 18 U.S.C. 1350 reaches every periodic report with financial statements, while 404(a) is annual.
Exam cue: on a 10-Q, look for the 302 and 906 certifications; the 404 internal control report appears once a year, in the 10-K.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Conduct toward the auditor
questions.question: Following the CEO's direction, a regional sales vice president hides from the auditors a side letter giving a customer return rights, to keep revenue in the quarter. Which provision MOST directly prohibits this?

options.A: Section 304, which makes officers repay bonuses after misconduct
options.B: Section 302, which requires officers to disclose fraud to auditors
options.C: Section 307, which requires lawyers to report violations internally
options.D: Section 303, which bars misleading the auditor to distort statements

questions.key_concept: Section 303 bars officers, directors and those acting under their direction from fraudulently misleading or pressuring the auditor.
questions.pre_read: Ask which provision is aimed at conduct toward the auditor, and whether it reaches staff acting on an officer's instructions.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 303 makes it unlawful for an officer or director, or anyone acting under their direction, to fraudulently influence, coerce, manipulate or mislead the auditor to make the financial statements materially misleading. Hiding a side letter on the CEO's direction fits that prohibition. Section 302 is an officer certification that includes disclosing fraud; it does not itself prohibit misleading the auditor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because misconduct can lead to repayment. But Section 304 applies after a misconduct restatement and recovers CEO and CFO pay; it does not prohibit misleading auditors.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: officers certify they disclosed fraud to the auditors. But that is a certification duty; Section 303 is the provision that prohibits misleading the auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it concerns reporting violations. But Section 307 sets duties for attorneys practicing before the SEC, not for sales staff dealing with auditors.

tips: Eliminate: A and C. Section 304 recovers pay after a restatement, and Section 307 governs attorneys' internal reporting, not conduct toward auditors.
Final two: D beats B because Section 303 prohibits misleading the auditor, and it reaches anyone acting under an officer's direction.
Exam cue: pressure on, or deception of, the outside auditor by insiders or their staff points to Section 303.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 303 (Improper influence on conduct of audits)

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Amounts repaid
questions.question: A company restates its financial statements because misconduct caused material noncompliance with reporting requirements. Under Section 304, which CEO and CFO amounts are MOST clearly subject to reimbursement?

options.A: Base salary paid for each period the restatement covers
options.B: Incentive pay received in the three fiscal years before the restatement
options.C: Bonuses and stock-sale profits in the 12 months after first issuance
options.D: Any pay the audit committee links to the misconduct

questions.key_concept: Section 304 recovers CEO and CFO bonuses, incentive or equity pay and stock-sale profits from 12 months after first issuance.
questions.pre_read: Recall the look-back window Section 304 uses and the kinds of pay it reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 304 requires the CEO and CFO to reimburse bonuses and other incentive-based or equity-based pay received, and profits from selling company stock, during the 12 months after the misstated document was first publicly issued or filed. The three-year look-back reaching every executive officer belongs to the Rule 10D-1 recovery policy, a separate no-fault listing rule.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because salary is the largest pay item. But Section 304 reaches bonuses, incentive or equity pay and stock-sale profits, not base salary.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: this describes the Rule 10D-1 recovery policy. Section 304 uses a 12-month window after first issuance or filing and covers only the CEO and CFO.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit committee oversees reporting. But Section 304 sets the amounts by statute; it does not leave them to committee judgment.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Section 304 does not reach base salary, and the statute, not the audit committee, defines what is repaid.
Final two: C beats B because Section 304 uses the 12 months after first issuance; the three-year look-back is the Rule 10D-1 policy.
Exam cue: misconduct restatement plus CEO and CFO plus a 12-month window points to Section 304, not the Rule 10D-1 clawback.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 304 (Forfeiture of certain bonuses and profits)

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Trade during a plan freeze
questions.question: During a ten-business-day freeze that stops every 401(k) participant from trading company stock, a director sells shares received as director pay, at a profit. What is the MOST accurate consequence?

options.A: The director's profit from the sale belongs to the issuer
options.B: The SEC must sue within 60 days to recover the profit
options.C: The sale stands, since the director meant no harm
options.D: The sale stands, since the director has no plan account

questions.key_concept: Profits from a director's or executive officer's trade during a pension blackout belong to the issuer, regardless of intent.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the freeze is a blackout under the statute, then recall who is restricted and who gets any profit.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 306(a) makes it unlawful for a director or executive officer to sell stock acquired through that service during a blackout of more than three business days affecting at least half of plan participants. Any profit belongs to the issuer, whatever the director intended. The issuer recovers it; a shareholder may sue on the issuer's behalf if the issuer does not act within 60 days of a request.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: 60 days does appear in Section 306. But it is the time the issuer has before a shareholder may sue; the profit goes to the issuer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because many violations require intent. But Section 306(a) makes the profit recoverable irrespective of the director's intention.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the freeze affects plan participants. But the trading ban applies to directors and executive officers whether or not they hold plan accounts.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 306(a) disregards intent, and the ban reaches directors and executive officers whether or not they are plan participants.
Final two: A beats B because the profit belongs to the issuer, and 60 days is when a shareholder may sue on its behalf.
Exam cue: an insider trade during a pension blackout means the issuer recovers the profit, regardless of intent.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Attorneys and fair funds. First report
questions.question: An outside lawyer representing a listed company with no qualified legal compliance committee finds evidence of a material securities violation. Under Section 307, where must the lawyer report FIRST?

options.A: To the audit committee of the board of directors
options.B: To the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO
options.C: To the SEC's Division of Enforcement, in writing
options.D: Nowhere, because legal privilege keeps the evidence confidential

questions.key_concept: An attorney's report of a material violation goes first to the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO, then up the ladder.
questions.pre_read: Recall the order of the reporting ladder the Section 307 rule sets, and when the second rung applies.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 307 required SEC rules making an attorney who practices before the SEC for an issuer report evidence of a material violation up the ladder. Under 17 CFR 205.3(b), the first report goes to the chief legal officer, or to that officer and the CEO. Only if they fail to respond appropriately does the report go to the audit committee, another independent committee or the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the audit committee is the second rung. The rule sends the report there only after no appropriate response, or when reporting first would be futile.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC enforces securities law. But Section 307 sets an internal reporting ladder; it does not require a first report to the SEC.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because lawyers protect client confidences. But the rule requires reporting inside the company, and doing so does not breach privilege.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The Section 307 rule keeps the report inside the company, and reporting to its officers does not breach client confidences.
Final two: B beats A because the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO, comes first; the audit committee is the next rung.
Exam cue: attorney evidence of a violation climbs the ladder: chief legal officer or CEO first, then the audit committee or board.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Attorneys and fair funds. Where a penalty goes
questions.question: The SEC obtains both a disgorgement order and a civil penalty against a former CFO who misled investors. Under Section 308, what is the MOST accurate statement about the penalty?

options.A: It goes to the U.S. Treasury, while disgorgement alone reaches victims
options.B: It is paid to the company to make up its own losses
options.C: It is paid to the PCAOB to fund audit firm inspections
options.D: It is added to the disgorgement fund for the violation's victims

questions.key_concept: Under Section 308, the SEC can add a civil penalty to the disgorgement fund so it compensates victims.
questions.pre_read: Recall who Section 308 was written to benefit and what it allows the SEC to do with penalty money.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 308 provides that when the SEC obtains a disgorgement order and also a civil penalty against the same person, the penalty can, on the SEC's motion or at its direction, be added to the disgorgement fund for the victims. That is the fair funds rule. Section 308 also amended the provisions that sent such penalties to the U.S. Treasury, to allow this exception.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: civil penalties generally go to the Treasury. But Section 308 lets the SEC add the penalty to the disgorgement fund so victims receive it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the company may have been harmed too. But Section 308 directs the money toward the investors who were victims, through the disgorgement fund.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the PCAOB oversees auditors. But Section 308 concerns SEC actions against violators and funds for their victims, not PCAOB funding.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Fair funds serve the investors harmed by a violation, not the company's own losses or the PCAOB's budget.
Final two: D beats A because Section 308 lets the SEC add civil penalties to the disgorgement fund for victims.
Exam cue: a penalty steered to harmed investors through a disgorgement fund points to Section 308 fair funds.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings. Credit to an executive
questions.question: A retail chain that issues its own credit cards to shoppers reviews four proposals for its CFO. Under Section 402, which arrangement is MOST clearly permitted?

options.A: A low-rate relocation loan made through a foreign subsidiary
options.B: A personal loan the company arranges with a partner bank
options.C: A card account on the terms offered to the general public
options.D: A pre-2002 personal loan renewed this year on better terms

questions.key_concept: Section 402 bars personal loans to directors and executive officers, except ordinary-course consumer credit on public terms.
questions.pre_read: Recall the ways of providing credit Section 402 prohibits, and the conditions of its consumer credit exception.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 402 bars an issuer, directly or through a subsidiary, from extending, arranging or renewing personal loans to directors and executive officers. It excepts consumer credit, such as a credit card, made in the ordinary course of the issuer's consumer credit business, generally offered to the public, on terms no better than the public receives. A card account on public terms fits that exception; arranging a bank loan does not.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a foreign subsidiary seems outside the rule. But Section 402 covers credit extended directly or indirectly, including through any subsidiary.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the bank, not the company, would lend. But Section 402 also prohibits arranging an extension of credit for a director or executive officer.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because older loans were grandfathered. But that protection ends if the loan is renewed or materially modified after the Act.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Section 402 reaches credit through any subsidiary, and renewing an older loan ends its grandfathered status.
Final two: C beats B because ordinary-course consumer credit on public terms is excepted, while arranging a loan is itself prohibited.
Exam cue: an insider loan is barred whether made, arranged or renewed; ordinary-course consumer credit on public terms is the exception.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings. Reporting deadline
questions.question: A director of a listed company buys company shares on a Monday. Under Section 403, which deadline MOST accurately applies to reporting this change in ownership?

options.A: Within 10 days after the end of the month of the trade
options.B: Before the end of the second business day after the trade
options.C: Within 10 days after the director first joined the board
options.D: With the company's next quarterly report on Form 10-Q

questions.key_concept: Insiders report a change in ownership before the end of the second business day after the trade.
questions.pre_read: Separate the deadline for a first statement on becoming an insider from the deadline for later trades.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 403 rewrote Exchange Act Section 16(a). A director, officer or owner of more than 10 percent must report a change in ownership before the end of the second business day after the trade is executed, unless the SEC sets another time where two days is not feasible. Ten days applies to the initial statement after becoming an insider, not to later trades.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: monthly reporting sounds like a periodic duty. But Section 16(a) as amended requires change reports before the end of the second business day after the trade.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 10 days is a real Section 16(a) deadline. But it applies to the initial statement after becoming a director, not to later trades.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because quarterly reports disclose many changes. But insider ownership changes are filed separately and quickly, not with the Form 10-Q.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Ten days covers the initial statement on becoming an insider, and insider trades are reported separately from the 10-Q.
Final two: B beats A because Section 403 requires change reports by the end of the second business day, not on a monthly cycle.
Exam cue: an insider's change in holdings is due within two business days; the initial statement is due within 10 days.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 403(a) (Disclosures of transactions involving management and principal stockholders)

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. As-of date
questions.question: Management of a calendar-year company prepares its Section 404(a) report on internal control over financial reporting. As of which date is the effectiveness assessment MOST accurately made?

options.A: December 31, the end of the most recent fiscal year
options.B: Any date within 90 days before the annual report is filed
options.C: Across the whole fiscal year, from January through December
options.D: The date the audit firm signs its attestation report

questions.key_concept: Management assesses internal control over financial reporting as of the end of the most recent fiscal year.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether the assessment is a point-in-time conclusion or a period conclusion, and which point the statute names.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(a) and Item 308(a) require management to assess the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting as of the end of the most recent fiscal year. For a calendar-year company that is December 31. The 90-day window appears in Section 302's text on the officers' evaluation of internal controls, not in the 404(a) assessment, which is a point-in-time conclusion at year-end.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 302's text mentions an evaluation within 90 days before the report. Section 404(a) fixes the assessment at fiscal year-end instead.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing happens during the year. But the conclusion is stated as of a point in time, the fiscal year-end, not across the period.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the attestation follows the assessment. But the audit firm's signing date does not set management's as-of date; the fiscal year-end does.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The assessment is a point-in-time conclusion, and the audit firm's signing date does not set management's as-of date.
Final two: A beats B because Section 404(a) fixes the as-of date at fiscal year-end; the 90-day window comes from Section 302's text.
Exam cue: management's 404(a) assessment is as of fiscal year-end, even when testing runs throughout the year.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Smaller filer reports
questions.question: A non-accelerated filer that is not an emerging growth company prepares its fifth annual report. What does Section 404 MOST accurately require from its management and audit firm?

options.A: Management's report together with an auditor attestation report
options.B: No internal control report from management or the auditor
options.C: An auditor attestation report in place of management's report
options.D: Management's report, with no auditor attestation report

questions.key_concept: Non-accelerated filers file management's 404(a) report but are exempt from the 404(b) auditor attestation.
questions.pre_read: Recall which part of Section 404 the smaller-issuer exemption covers, and which part every annual-report filer keeps.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(a) requires management's internal control report in each annual report once a new registrant's transition period has passed. Section 404(c), added by Dodd-Frank Section 989G(a), exempts an issuer that is neither an accelerated nor a large accelerated filer from the auditor attestation in 404(b). So this non-accelerated filer files management's report without an auditor attestation.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: larger filers need both reports. But Section 404(c) exempts non-accelerated filers from the 404(b) auditor attestation.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because smaller filers get relief. But the exemption covers the auditor attestation alone; management's 404(a) report is still required.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors add assurance. But an attestation reports on management's assessment, so it cannot replace it, and here it is not required.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Every annual-report filer past its first year owes management's report, and an attestation reports on that assessment rather than replacing it.
Final two: D beats A because Section 404(c) exempts non-accelerated filers from the 404(b) auditor attestation.
Exam cue: non-accelerated filers and emerging growth companies skip 404(b), never 404(a).
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 404(c) (Exemption for smaller issuers); Dodd-Frank Act Section 989G(a) (Exemption for smaller issuers); 17 CFR 229.308(b) (Attestation report of the registered public accounting firm)

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Weakness fixed in the year
questions.question: In September, an accelerated filer's management finds a material weakness in revenue cutoff controls; replacement controls operate from November and test effective at December 31, its year-end. What may management MOST accurately conclude?

options.A: Controls were not effective, because a weakness existed before year-end
options.B: Controls were effective except for the revenue cutoff weakness
options.C: Controls were effective, as the weakness was remediated by year-end
options.D: No conclusion is possible until the auditor retests the new controls

questions.key_concept: A material weakness remediated and tested before fiscal year-end does not prevent an effective conclusion as of year-end.
questions.pre_read: Focus on the date the assessment speaks to, and on what the testing showed at that date.
questions.correct_explanation: Item 308(a) asks for management's assessment as of fiscal year-end, and management may not conclude controls are effective if a material weakness exists then. Release 33-8810 adds that when material weaknesses are remediated by year-end, management may conclude internal control is effective, while considering whether to disclose the remediated weakness. Here testing shows the fix worked at December 31.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a material weakness did exist in September. But the assessment is as of year-end, and this one was remediated and tested by then.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems candid. But SEC guidance says management should not qualify its conclusion with exceptions; it states effective or not effective.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditors test controls too. But management makes its own year-end conclusion; the auditor's work does not delay or replace it.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. SEC guidance bars except-for conclusions, and management concludes on its own evidence without waiting for the auditor.
Final two: C beats A because the 404(a) assessment is as of year-end, and a weakness remediated and tested by then does not block an effective conclusion.
Exam cue: judge material weaknesses at the as-of date. Open at year-end means not effective; fixed and tested before it allows effective.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Rating a failed review
questions.question: Management finds the review of large manual journal entries did not operate all year, yet no misstatement resulted, and the CFO says this cannot be a material weakness. Which response is MOST accurate?

options.A: Severity turns on the material misstatements actually found
options.B: Severity turns on the risk that a material misstatement is missed
options.C: Severity is set by the external auditor, not by management
options.D: Severity turns on how many separate controls failed this year

questions.key_concept: Deficiency severity depends on the reasonable possibility of a material misstatement going unprevented or undetected, not on actual errors.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the material weakness definition measures: what happened, or what could happen.
questions.correct_explanation: A material weakness exists when there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis (Rule 12b-2). Release 33-8810 states that severity does not depend on whether a misstatement actually occurred. A key review that failed all year over large manual entries can be a material weakness even though no error was found.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: actual errors are strong evidence of a deficiency. But severity rests on what could be missed, so finding no misstatement does not settle it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors assess deficiencies too. But management evaluates severity for its own 404(a) report under SEC rules and guidance.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because several failures can combine. But one failed control can be a material weakness; severity rests on likelihood and size, not a count.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Management rates severity for its own report, and severity depends on likelihood and magnitude rather than on counting failed controls.
Final two: B beats A because the definition asks whether a material misstatement could go unprevented or undetected, not whether one occurred.
Exam cue: when a stem says no error was found, ask what could have been missed; severity follows the potential, not the actual.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Ethics code, financial expert, SEC review and real-time disclosure. Committee without an expert
questions.question: A listed company's board determines that no audit committee member meets the SEC's definition of an audit committee financial expert. What does Section 407 MOST accurately require?

options.A: Disclose that the committee has none and explain why
options.B: Disclose that the committee has none, giving no reasons
options.C: Appoint a qualified expert to the committee before filing
options.D: Name the committee's most experienced member as its expert

questions.key_concept: Section 407 is disclose-or-explain: name the financial expert, or state there is none and explain why.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether Section 407 requires the company to have an expert or to disclose something, and what that disclosure must include.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 407 and Item 407(d)(5) are disclose-or-explain rules. The company discloses whether the board has determined that at least one audit committee financial expert serves on the committee; if none does, it must say so and explain why. The Act does not require the company to have an expert, so the explanation, not an appointment, is what the rule demands.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the company must disclose that it has no expert. But Item 407(d)(5) also requires it to explain why it has none.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an expert strengthens the committee. But Section 407 requires disclosure, not appointment; a company may lack an expert if it explains why.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because someone must fill the role. But the expert must have every attribute the SEC lists; naming an unqualified member would misstate the disclosure.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 407 requires disclosure rather than appointment, and a member without the SEC's attributes cannot be named as the expert.
Final two: A beats B because the rule requires an explanation of why the committee has no financial expert.
Exam cue: Sections 406 and 407 are disclose-or-explain: say whether you have it, and if not, say why.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Ethics code, financial expert, SEC review and real-time disclosure. Waiver for an officer
questions.question: A company's board grants its CFO a waiver from the conflict-of-interest provision of its code of ethics for senior financial officers. What does Section 406 MOST accurately require?

options.A: Seek SEC approval of the waiver before it takes effect
options.B: Report the waiver in the next annual report on Form 10-K
options.C: Disclose the waiver immediately, on Form 8-K or online
options.D: Keep the waiver internal, since adopting a code is optional

questions.key_concept: Any change in or waiver of the code of ethics for senior financial officers must be disclosed immediately.
questions.pre_read: Separate the rule about having a code from the rule about changing or waiving one, and recall its timing.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 406(b) requires immediate disclosure of any change in or waiver of the code of ethics for senior financial officers, by filing Form 8-K or by Internet or other electronic means. Item 406 lets a company use its website for this if its annual report says so. Waiting for the next Form 10-K misses the immediate-disclosure requirement.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the SEC oversees disclosure. But Section 406 requires disclosure of the waiver, not SEC approval before it takes effect.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the annual report does cover the code. But changes and waivers must be disclosed immediately, not held for the next 10-K.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Section 406 is disclose-or-explain for adopting a code. But once a code exists, any waiver for senior financial officers must be disclosed.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Section 406 requires disclosure rather than SEC approval, and the disclose-or-explain choice on adopting a code does not cover waivers.
Final two: C beats B because Section 406(b) requires immediate disclosure of waivers, not disclosure in the next annual report.
Exam cue: a change in or waiver of the senior financial officers' code means immediate disclosure on Form 8-K or online.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Ethics code, financial expert, SEC review and real-time disclosure. Review cycle
questions.question: The CFO of a listed company that has filed Section 13(a) reports for years asks how often the SEC must review them. Under Section 408, what is the GREATEST interval allowed between reviews?

options.A: At least once every year
options.B: At least once every five years
options.C: Whenever a material restatement is issued
options.D: At least once every three years

questions.key_concept: The SEC must review each reporting issuer's disclosures at least once every three years.
questions.pre_read: Recall the statutory floor for SEC review and the role of the scheduling factors Section 408 lists.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 408 requires the SEC to review the disclosures of issuers reporting under Section 13(a), including their financial statements, on a regular and systematic basis. Section 408(c) sets the floor: no issuer may be reviewed less often than once every three years. Restatements, volatility and size are scheduling factors that can bring a review sooner, not the sole trigger.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many issuers are reviewed more often than the minimum. But Section 408 sets the floor at once every three years, not every year.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because five years appears elsewhere in SOX, in audit partner rotation. But Section 408 sets the review floor at three years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because restatements are a review factor. But Section 408(b) lists them as scheduling factors; the three-year floor applies to every reporting issuer.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Five years is not the review floor, and restatements only affect scheduling within the three-year cycle.
Final two: D beats A because Section 408(c) requires review at least once every three years; yearly review is not the statutory minimum.
Exam cue: SEC review of each reporting issuer's filings happens at least once every three years under Section 408.
